text: Fifteen years ago he had come to Kew with Lily and had begged her to marry him, and as they sat by a lake, a dragonfly kept circling round and round them in the heat. <break time="0.8s" /> How clearly he could still see the dragonfly, and her shoe with the square silver buckle at the toe, moving impatiently while he spoke, so that he knew her answer without looking up at her face. <break time="0.8s" /> He had told himself that if the dragonfly settled on a leaf she would say Yes at once, but it went round and round and never settled anywhere, and Lily had not married him. <break time="0.8s" /> Turning to his wife at last, Simon asked her whether she ever thought of the past, and he confessed that he had been thinking of Lily, the woman he might have married. <break time="0.8s" /> Far from minding, Eleanor answered calmly that one always thought of the past in a garden where men and women lay under the trees, for they seemed to be the ghosts of ones own happiness. <break time="0.8s" /> For her part, she remembered six little girls sitting before their easels by a lake twenty years ago, painting the first red water lilies she had ever seen, when suddenly a kiss fell on the back of her neck. <break time="0.8s" /> It had been given, she said, by an old gray haired woman with a wart on her nose, and it was the mother of all her kisses all her life. <break time="0.8s" /> Come, Caroline, come, Hubert, Eleanor called, and the family walked on, four abreast, until they diminished in size among the trees and looked half transparent in the trembling sunlight and shade.
